name: Palazzo Parisio
architectural_style: Belle Époque palace constructed in 1898 over the footprint of a 17th-century predecessor palazzo; the 4th Marquis of Scicluna commissioned a comprehensive Italianate reconstruction producing the current façade, grand marble staircase, ballroom, and formal reception suite; interiors display the full decorative vocabulary of late-19th-century aristocratic design — frescoed ceilings, gilded mouldings, decorative panelling, and imported Carrara marble; the formal garden of approximately 5,000 square metres follows baroque principles of axial symmetry with geometric box-hedge parterres, classical fountains, and marble statuary arranged on a central axis

opening_hours.seasonal_note: The palazzo opens Tuesday to Sunday; it is frequently closed for private events and functions, so it is strongly recommended to check current availability at palazzoparisio.com or by telephone before travelling. Last entry is 1 hour before closing. The garden may remain accessible when the state rooms are reserved for private events — call ahead to confirm.

best_season: October to May — Malta summers (July–August) are very hot; the formal garden is most attractive in spring flowers; the palace interior is year-round
accessibility: The ground-floor state rooms and garden are accessible to visitors with limited mobility. The grand marble staircase leads to upper floors; step-free access to the upper rooms is not available.
tagline: A Belle Époque aristocratic palace in Naxxar — Malta's finest private residence, with a grand ballroom, frescoed ceilings, and a formal baroque garden open to the public
highlights: The grand ballroom — the palazzo's ceremonial centrepiece, with a frescoed ceiling, gilded mouldings, and proportions that express the Scicluna family's ambitions at their peak; one of the most lavish 19th-century aristocratic interiors surviving in Malta

The formal baroque-style garden of approximately 5,000 square metres — geometric box-hedge parterres, classical fountains, and marble statuary on a central axis; a rare example of formal European garden design maintained in Malta
The grand marble staircase — the palazzo's entrance sequence, a double-flight staircase in Carrara marble beneath a frescoed vault that establishes the decorative register of the state rooms above

The suite of state reception rooms — salon, dining rooms, and reception halls with their original 1898 frescoed ceilings, decorative panelling, period furnishings, and imported marble; a coherent example of late-19th-century aristocratic domestic taste

Naxxar village setting — the palazzo occupies the heart of a baroque Maltese hill town 10 kilometres north of Valletta; the approach through limestone streets of baroque churches and traditional townhouses is part of the experience
description:
Palazzo Parisio stands at the heart of Naxxar, a Maltese hill town of baroque churches and limestone townhouses ten kilometres north of Valletta. The palazzo visible today is primarily the creation of the 4th Marquis of Scicluna, who commissioned a sweeping Belle Époque reconstruction in 1898, transforming an earlier 17th-century palazzo into one of the grandest private residences in Maltese history. The result is a palace that reads simultaneously as a product of European fin-de-siècle taste and as an authentically Maltese aristocratic achievement — the scale and ambition of a northern Italian palazzo set within the compact streets of a Maltese village.

The palace interiors follow the full programme of a late-19th-century residence of means. The entrance sequence begins with the grand marble staircase — double-flight, Carrara marble, set beneath a frescoed vault — which establishes the decorative register of the rooms above. The grand ballroom is the ceremonial centrepiece: a large, high-ceilinged room with a frescoed ceiling, gilded mouldings, and the proportions of a space designed for entertaining on a serious social scale. The salon, dining rooms, and reception halls beyond continue in the same register — frescoed ceilings, decorative panelling, period furnishings, and imported marble throughout.

The formal garden of approximately 5,000 square metres completes the visit. The garden follows baroque principles of axial symmetry, with geometric box-hedge parterres, classical fountains, and marble statuary arranged along central axes. For Malta, where the island's geology and climate make large-scale formal gardens exceptional, Palazzo Parisio's garden is a rarity: a substantial, well-maintained example of European baroque garden design surviving in private hands and open to the public. Spring planting — particularly from March to May — brings the parterres to their most photogenic state.

The palazzo today operates as a prestigious private event venue — dinners, weddings, and corporate functions occupy the state rooms regularly — while remaining partially open to paying visitors. The practical consequence is that opening days and room access can vary; it is advisable to check availability at palazzoparisio.com before travelling. When the palace is open, the self-guided visit takes approximately one to one and a half hours for both the state rooms and the garden circuit.

For visitors exploring Malta's historic interiors, Palazzo Parisio stands as the island's finest example of aristocratic domestic architecture from the Belle Époque period — a counterpoint to the baroque grandeur of Valletta's Grand Master's Palace and the medieval austerity of Mdina. The atmosphere is intimate rather than monumental: this was a working private home designed for a family of means, and its human scale distinguishes it from the grander palatial environments of the Mediterranean.
history:
The site in Naxxar was originally occupied by a palazzo belonging to Grand Master Vilhena of the Knights of Malta, one of the senior figures of the Order in the early 18th century. The property passed through several hands over the subsequent decades before the Scicluna family — one of the most prominent banking and commercial dynasties in 19th-century Malta — acquired the estate. The 4th Marquis of Scicluna undertook the wholesale reconstruction that produced the current palazzo in 1898, engaging architects and craftsmen to create a residence equal to the finest contemporary aristocratic homes in Italianate Europe. The reconstruction preserved the earlier building's spatial footprint while completely transforming its interiors and formal garden into the Belle Époque composition visible today.

The Scicluna family maintained Palazzo Parisio as their primary Maltese residence through the early 20th century, using its ballroom and reception rooms for the social functions that defined aristocratic life on the island in the years before and after Maltese independence in 1964. The palazzo's subsequent conversion into a semi-public venue — retaining private event functions while opening the state rooms and garden to visitors — has allowed the building's upkeep to continue while making one of Malta's most significant historic interiors accessible for the first time to a wider public.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** From Valletta, bus route 41 serves Naxxar directly (approximately 30 minutes). By car from Valletta, Naxxar is approximately 10 kilometres north via the Regional Road; parking is available on Triq il-Palazz and the surrounding village streets. From St Julian's or Sliema, bus routes connecting through the Birkirkara area serve Naxxar in approximately 25 minutes.

**Tickets:** Walk-up admission is €15 for adults, €8 for children, covering the palace state rooms and the formal garden; purchase at the door on the day. Note that the palazzo operates as a private event venue and may be fully closed on any given day — check current availability at palazzoparisio.com before travelling.

**Practical tips:** The palazzo is closed on Mondays. Arrive in the morning to maximise the chance of accessing both state rooms and garden before any afternoon event closures. The garden is at its best from March to May when spring planting is in colour; the palace interiors can be visited year-round when open. Malta summers (July–August) are intensely hot — if visiting in high season, the morning slot significantly reduces the midday heat in the open garden.

**Combine with:** [Mdina](/castles/malta/mdina) — the medieval walled city 8 kilometres southwest of Naxxar, the original capital of Malta and one of the best-preserved medieval urban enclosures in the Mediterranean; reachable by car in 15 minutes or by bus via Birkirkara.

faqs.question: Can I visit Palazzo Parisio independently or do I need to book a tour?
faqs.answer: Palazzo Parisio operates as a self-guided visit — there is no compulsory guided tour, and visitors explore the state rooms and garden at their own pace. Entry tickets are purchased at the door (€15 adult, €8 child) when the palazzo is open. Because the palazzo doubles as a private event venue, it can close at short notice for functions; checking current availability at palazzoparisio.com or by telephone before travelling is strongly recommended.

faqs.question: Is the garden open separately from the palace state rooms?
faqs.answer: On days when the state rooms are reserved for a private function, the formal garden may remain accessible. In practice, access to the garden independently of the palace varies by event; call the palazzo directly to confirm. The garden visit alone — the formal baroque parterres, fountains, and statuary — takes approximately 30–40 minutes and is worth the detour during spring flowering season (March to May).

faqs.question: How does Palazzo Parisio fit into Malta's wider heritage landscape?
faqs.answer: Palazzo Parisio is the island's outstanding example of a private aristocratic residence from the Belle Époque period — distinct from the grander, more public architecture of Valletta (Grand Master's Palace, St John's Co-Cathedral) and the medieval walled character of Mdina. It fills the domestic scale that those monumental sites cannot: an insight into how a wealthy Maltese family lived at the turn of the 20th century. For visitors spending more than two or three days in Malta, it adds a genuinely different register to the standard heritage itinerary.
